messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas sat in the corner of his agency’s intake office, tracing the worn edge of his desk while the memory of the assault remained locked behind his teeth. Two years prior, a man had dragged him into a narrow maintenance corridor behind the county counseling center, pinning him against concrete walls while a single flickering bulb cast long, suffocating shadows. Thomas knew exactly what had happened to him, yet whenever he tried to articulate it to his wife, his throat closed and the words dissolved into a thick, choking silence. When the recollection surfaced unbidden, a heavy wave of shame washed over him, immediately followed by the same visceral terror he had felt in that darkened hallway. That unnameable horror did not fade; it anchored itself to his nervous system, directly fueling his threat appraisal. He found himself scanning crowded clinic corridors, his eyes darting toward every shadow, convinced that footsteps behind him signaled the same predator returning. When he couldn’t locate anyone, his anxiety simply migrated to new vulnerabilities, steering him away from unfamiliar neighborhoods where he couldn’t map the exits or assess the sightlines. Whenever the shame and terror crept back in, Thomas’s mind immediately scrambled to control the intrusion. He tried to force the images out of his head, pressing his palms against his temples until his forehead ached, but the suppression only left his baseline arousal elevated. In the quiet hours, the unresolved rage crystallized into a relentless loop, keeping him awake as he replayed the event and fixated on how to make the man who hurt him pay. These mental efforts did not passively coexist with his symptoms; the very act of chasing revenge fantasies and pushing the trauma from his awareness actively pushed him toward avoidance. He stopped taking field visits, refusing to enter any small meeting room or conference space without propping the door wide open, convinced that confinement would strip him of control again. The hyper vigilance that had taken root quickly reshaped his daily routines. When things ran late—a delayed elevator, a traffic jam on the route to his familiar practice—his body assumed disaster was already unfolding, which drove him further into rigid avoidance and mental suppression. His refusal to enter enclosed spaces and his relentless scanning of parking lots only left his baseline arousal elevated, which in turn made his threat monitoring more aggressive. He caught himself checking every rearview mirror, pacing the perimeter of familiar buildings, and fixating on potential ambush points, each avoidance tactic feeding the very alarm system he was trying to quiet. The fear of being trapped became non-negotiable, and his steering clear of unfamiliar places only ensured that his nervous system never learned safety was possible outside his routine. That perpetually activated alertness did not remain one-way; it looped back into the trauma network. The constant checking behind him and the assumption that delays meant danger kept his nervous system in a state of high alert, which made the original memories surface more frequently and with greater intensity. Each time the shame and terror returned, his inability to find words for what happened left him feeling fractured, and the recurring threat appraisal kept him trapped in the same defensive posture. Over eighteen months, these habits calcified. Thomas, who once made house calls across three counties, now restricted himself to the agency’s main floor, telling his colleagues he was focusing on administrative work. His wife kept trying to draw him into shared outings, but he withdrew into rigid schedules and defensive explanations, terrified that surrendering control would leave him powerless again. What finally pushed him to the clinic was a panic attack during a site inspection when the fire alarm forced him into a cramped stairwell. He realized he was no longer helping others because he was too busy surviving his own past. He hoped therapy could untangle the shame from the terror, not so he could forget what happened, but so he could stop letting a decades-old violation dictate where he walked, who he trusted, and how he lived his days.
